--- title: "Getting Started: Three Ways of Running Python" --- ::: {.callout-tip} ## Learning Objectives - Set up your working folder in VS Code - Understand the three main ways of running Python: **Way 1 (Scripts)**, **Way 2 (the Console)**, and **Way 3 (Jupyter Notebooks)** - Find out what a terminal actually is - See the difference between code cells and text cells in a Jupyter Notebook - Try out each of the three ways for yourself - Get a simple idea of what a Jupyter "kernel" does ::: ## Overview Before you write any Python code, it helps to know that there are several different ways of actually running it. In this lesson, you will meet three of them. Each one suits a different situation — a bit like how you might send a text message for something quick, write a letter for something you want to keep, or put together a scrapbook when you want words and pictures together. By the end of this lesson, you will have tried all three for yourself. ## Setting Up Your Working Folder in VS Code Before you run any code, VS Code needs to know which folder on your computer you are working in. This is called your **working directory**. (These instructions use Linux. If you are using Windows or a Mac, everything will look almost the same.) 1. Open VS Code. 2. At the top, click **File → Open Folder...** 3. Find and select the `scripts` folder that came with your course materials. 4. Click **Open**. This matters because, by default, Python will look for any other files it needs inside this folder, and will save anything it creates back into this folder too. We will go into much more detail about exactly how this works later in the course — for now, just make sure this is the folder you have open. ## What Is a Terminal? In the last section, you pressed a play button to run a script, and a box appeared at the bottom of your screen asking you to type something in. That box has a name: it is called the **terminal**. A terminal is simply a plain text window where you type instructions for your computer, instead of clicking on menus and icons with your mouse. It looks a little old-fashioned, but it is one of the most useful tools you will use as a programmer in particular because it is much quicker than using the mouse. You can open a terminal in VS Code at any time by clicking **Terminal → New Terminal** at the top of the screen (or by pressing **Ctrl + `**). Because you already opened the `scripts` folder, your terminal will start there too. ## Way 1: Running Python Using a Script A **script** is simply a text file with your Python code saved inside it, ending in `.py`. Think of it as a recipe you have written down: you can follow it once, put it away, and come back to run it again whenever you like. This makes scripts the best choice when you want to save your work properly. There are two equally valid ways to run a script: - Press the **Play button** in VS Code, just as you did in the last section. - Type the command yourself directly into the terminal: ```bash python my_script.py ``` Whichever way you choose, the output appears in the same place: the terminal window at the bottom of your screen. That is the default behaviour of a script — everything it produces shows up there. ::: {.callout-tip} ## A note on Python vs Python 3 Depending on how Python is set up on your computer, you might need to type `python3` instead of `python`. If one does not work, try the other. Note that on your own machines, you do not want to be running things on the default python that comes pre-installed. This is because you do not want to mess with the setup that many other software including your operating system might use. We will cover more about this later in the environments section. ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Working directory If running your script is not working from the terminal check that you are in the correct working directory. You need to be in the correct directory to run a python script from the terminal. As we opened the scripts foldr in VSCode, it should automatically that as the working directory - e.g. where the expense_calculator.py is located ::: **Example:** Imagine you saved a file called `hello.py` containing one line of code: ```python print("This message came from a script!") ``` If you ran this file — either by pressing Play, or by typing `python hello.py` into the terminal — this is what your terminal window might actually look like: ```{=html}
you@scripts % python hello.py This message came from a script! you@scripts %
``` Notice that the message appears right below the command you typed. That is what "running" a script actually means: Python reads your file from top to bottom, carries out each instruction, and the terminal shows you the result. ## Way 2: Running Python Using the Console (REPL) Sometimes you do not want to save anything at all — you just want to try a quick idea and see what happens. That is exactly what the **Python Console** is for. The console is sometimes called a **REPL**, which is a simple way of describing four things it does, one after another: - **R**ead — it reads the line of code you type - **E**valuate — it works out the answer straight away - **P**rint — it shows you the answer on the screen - **L**oop — it waits patiently for your next line This instant back-and-forth makes the console brilliant for quick tests. The catch is that nothing you type is saved — as soon as you close it, it is gone, a bit like a chat message that disappears the moment you close the app. **Opening the console** 1. In your VS Code terminal, type `python` (or `python3`) and press Enter. 2. You will see three arrows, `>>>`, waiting for you. 3. When you are finished, type `exit()` and press Enter to leave the console and return to your ordinary terminal. **Example:** Here is what it would actually look like if you typed two lines into the console, one after another, and then exited: ```{=html}
you@scripts % python Python 3.11.0 (default, Oct 24 2026, 08:01:31) Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information. >>> print("Typed straight into the console!") Typed straight into the console! >>> print("And here is a second line!") And here is a second line! >>> exit() you@scripts %
``` Notice how each answer appears immediately after you press Enter, and Python is straight back with `>>>`, ready for your next line. Once you type `exit()`, the `>>>` disappears and you are back in your ordinary terminal. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Working directory *If you're interested in using the terminal more, for example to navigate file systems and automate tasks - attend the training facilities unix/command line course* ::: ## Way 3: Running Python Using Jupyter Notebooks When you run a piece of code inside a Jupyter Notebook, the result appears directly underneath it, and both stay together, permanently, in the same file — a record of exactly what you wrote and what it produced. A **Jupyter Notebook** is a file ending in `.ipynb` that mixes code and writing together, split up into separate blocks called **cells** — a bit like a scrapbook, where some pages hold your working and other pages hold your notes. Don't worry about installing anything — the software and extensions you need have already been set up for you. **Two kinds of cell** - **Code cells** hold Python code. When you run one, Python carries out the instructions and shows the result directly underneath — just like the terminal examples above. - **Text cells** (also called Markdown cells) hold ordinary writing: titles, explanations, or notes. They do not run any code at all; they are simply there for you to read. **Example:** If you typed the following into a code cell and ran it: ```python print("This is a notebook cell speaking!") ``` This is exactly what you would see, with the code and its result kept together in one place: ::: {#8ed1a97a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} print("This is a notebook cell speaking!") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` This is a notebook cell speaking! ``` ::: ::: Unlike the console, this stays exactly where it is when you save the file, so you (or anyone else) can come back later and see both the code and its result side by side. **Opening a notebook** *Option A — Inside VS Code* 1. Click **File → New File...** 2. Choose **Jupyter Notebook** (or create a new file and save it as `notebook.ipynb`). 3. An interactive notebook page will open inside VS Code. *Option B — In your web browser* 1. Open a terminal in VS Code. 2. Type the following and press Enter: ```bash jupyter notebook ``` 3. A browser tab will open automatically, showing your notebook. **What is a kernel?** When you open a notebook, you will be asked to choose a **kernel**. In simple terms, the kernel loads the specific setup you need — including the correct version of Python — and keeps track of the current state of your work: it remembers every variable and every result you have created so far in that notebook. In the top-right corner of your notebook in VS Code, click **Select Kernel** and choose the course option provided. ## Exercises Now it is your turn to try each way for yourself. ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Script Create a new file in your `scripts` folder named `hello.py`. Inside it, write the line `print("hello world")`, save the file, then run it from the terminal by typing `python hello.py`. What happens? ::: {.callout-answer} When you run `hello.py`, Python reads through the file from top to bottom and carries out the `print("hello world")` command. This displays the text: hello world directly in your terminal window, underneath the command you typed. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Python console Open the Python console in VS Code. Type `print("hello world")`. What happens? ::: {.callout-answer} When the command `print("hello world")` is entered into the Python console and executed, Python immediately evaluates the statement and displays the text: hello world right away, with no file being saved anywhere. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Jupyter Notebook Open a new Jupyter Notebook in VS Code and save it as `practice.ipynb` in your `scripts` folder. In the first code cell, type `print("hello world")`, then run it by clicking the Play button next to the cell (or pressing **Shift + Enter**). What happens? ::: {.callout-answer} When you run the cell, Python evaluates `print("hello world")` and displays the text: hello world directly beneath the cell. Because it is a notebook, this result is saved alongside your code when you save the file, so it will still be there the next time you open it. ::: ::: ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Which Way Would You Choose? For each scenario below, decide whether **Way 1 (Script)**, **Way 2 (Console)**, or **Way 3 (Notebook)** would suit it best. 1. You want to quickly check what `12 * 7` equals before moving on with your work. 2. You are writing a program that checks tomorrow's weather, and you want to be able to run it again every morning. 3. You are putting together a piece of coursework that needs to show your code, a chart, and a written explanation of what you found, all in one place. 4. A friend asks you what a certain line of Python code does, and you want to test it there and then, without saving anything. 5. You are teaching yourself a new topic, and want to try out several short pieces of code one after another, jotting down a note next to each one so you can revise from it before an exam next week. 6. You have written a program that needs to run automatically every night at 2am, without anyone there to click a button or type anything. ::: {.callout-answer} 1. **Way 2 (Console)** — a quick, one-off check with nothing you need to save. 2. **Way 1 (Script)** — something permanent that you will want to run again and again, unattended. 3. **Way 3 (Notebook)** — your code, its results, and your written explanation all need to sit together. 4. **Way 2 (Console)** — fast, temporary, and no file required. 5. **Way 3 (Notebook)** — this is trickier than it first looks: although you are trying things out one after another, the console will not do, because you need to keep both the code and your written notes together for later. That combination of code plus writing, saved for future reference, is exactly what a notebook is for. 6. **Way 1 (Script)** — this is the hardest one: a notebook needs a kernel and someone to click "run", and the console needs someone typing live, so neither can run unattended. Only a saved script can be triggered automatically, with no one present, which is why scripts are the standard choice for anything that needs to run on its own. ::: ::: ## Summary: Three Ways of Running Python ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key Takeaways - **Way 1 — Scripts (`.py` files):** Saved text files, run either by pressing Play in VS Code or by typing `python script_name.py` in the terminal. Best for programs you want to keep, reuse, or run automatically. - **Way 2 — The Console (REPL):** An interactive terminal screen that runs each line instantly. Best for quick, temporary checks. - **Way 3 — Jupyter Notebooks (`.ipynb` files):** Interactive pages mixing code cells and text cells, keeping code and results together permanently. Best for step-by-step work, projects, and notes. :::
